To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) CGAs, the most abundant poly-phenols in coffee, are capable of interacting with the oncogenic Ras protein, and that (b) this interaction is likely to be responsible for the chemoprotective properties of CGA-containing extracts from coffee beans.
CGAs are potent inhibitors of Ras proteins, the main driver of human cancer, and that coffee extracts are a good source of these natural compounds.
CGAs are able to interact with Ras proteins, and that this interaction is responsible for their biological effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of CGAs and coffee polyphenols as chemoprotectors.
the identification of the active components of green coffee beans and roasted coffee, which are responsible for their anti-carcinogenetic activity.
the elucidation of molecular mechanisms at the basis of the biological activity of CGAs, which are the main polyphenols in coffee.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the consumption of coffee, and in particular the main polyphenolic constituent 5-O-caffeoylquinic acid, could be beneficial to prevent the onset of cancer, particularly in the breast and colon, by inhibiting the activation of oncogenic Ras proteins.
CGA, as well as coffee extracts, are able to inhibit Ras proteins by binding to the effector binding domain, and thus preventing the interaction with Ras effectors.

CGAs and natural coffee extracts are potent inhibitors of oncogenic Ras proteins, and their effects are due to a direct interaction with the switch I region of Ras proteins, which is crucial for their oncogenic activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the anti-Ras activity of CGAs is due to their ability to interact with the oncogenic Ras proteins and to induce their conformational change, which leads to the loss of their ability to activate signaling pathways that are involved in cell proliferation.
CGAs are potent inhibitors of the Ras oncogene.

the CGA caffeoylquinic acid (CQA) and its derivatives, as well as coffee extracts, are able to bind to the oncogenic Ras proteins, RasG12V and RasQ61L, and to inhibit their interaction with effector proteins such as Raf and PIK3.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the CGA 5-O-caffeoylquinic acid (5-CA), which occurs in high amounts in coffee, is able to interact with the oncogenic Ras proteins and to prevent their interaction with the downstream effector protein Raf.
CGAs, and in particular 5-O-caffeoylquinic acid, can bind to the oncogenic Ras protein, thus inhibiting its interaction with the downstream effector protein Raf-1 and its subsequent activation.

the polyphenolic fraction of green coffee beans, and in particular 5-O-caffeoylquinic acid (5-O-CA), can inhibit the oncogenic Ras protein by binding to the Ras binding domain (RBD) of the Ras effector protein RalGDS.
